'''Frederick Colvig Anson'''<ref>{{cite web |title=Frederick Colvig Anson — Born 1933, Los Angeles County, California |url=https://californiabirthindex.org/birth/frederick_colvig_anson_born_1933_1579179 |website=CaliforniaBirthIndex.org |access-date=11 August 2026}}</ref> (February 17, 1933 – May 22, 2024) was an American [[electrochemist]] and a long-time professor at the [[California Institute of Technology]].

He received an [[honorary degree]] from the Paris Diderot University in 1933.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2023-03-21 |title=Fred C. Anson {{!}} Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering |url=https://cce.caltech.edu/people/fred-c-anson |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230321221707/https://cce.caltech.edu/people/fred-c-anson |archive-date=March 21, 2023 |access-date=2025-02-01 |website=cce.caltech.edu}}</ref> He was an Instructor at Caltech between 1957 and 1958; Assistant Professor between 1958 and 1962, Associate Professor between 1962 and 1968, a Professor between 1968 and 1995, an Elizabeth W. Gilloon Gilloon Professor between 1995 and 2001, a Gilloon Professor [[Emeritus]] from 2001 until his death in 2024. He was an executive officer for Chemistry at Caltech between 1973 and 1977, and the chairman at Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering between 1984 and 1994.<ref name=":0" /> He received an honorary doctorate from the [[Sorbonne University|Sorbonne]] in 1993.<ref name=":1" />

He was interested in the behavior of reactants on the surface of electrodes.<ref name=":1" /> During his lifetime he published more than 350 scientific papers.<ref name=":1" />

== Early life and education ==
Anson was born on February 17, 1933 in [[Los Angeles]]<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Fesenmaier |first=Kimm |date=2024-06-20 |title=Fred C. Anson (BS '54), 1933–2024 |url=https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/fred-c-anson-long-bs-54-19332024 |access-date=2025-02-01 |website=California Institute of Technology |language=en}}</ref> and grew up in California's Wilmar (now [[South San Gabriel, California|South San Gabriel]]).<ref name=":1" /><ref name="Wizards">{{Cite web|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times-mr-wizards-2-nam/203453066/|title=Mr. Wizards: 2 Named to Prestigious National Academy|date=May 29, 1988|first1=Berkley|last1=Hudson|pages=Section S, Part IX, pages 1, 5|work=The Los Angeles Times|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> There, as a kid, he delivered the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' as his first job.<ref name=":1" /><ref name="Scholar">{{Cite web|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times-times-carrier-scho/203454578/|title=Times Carrier Scholar Wins Honors at Caltech|date=June 14, 1954|pages=5|work=The Los Angeles Times|via=newspapers.com}}</ref> He attended [[Mark Keppel High School]] where he was encouraged by a teacher, a [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]] alumni, to apply for the university.<ref name=":1" /> It was in one of his visit with this teacher, that he attended a talk by [[Robert A. Millikan]] on Caltech's campus.<ref name=":1" /> He enrolled in 1950 and was awarded a scholarship by the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'', available exclusively to paper carriers, which covered Caltech's $600 annual tuition.<ref name="Scholar"/><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=2024-05-24 |title=Fred C. Anson (BS '54), 1933–2024 |url=https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/fred-c-anson-bs-54-19332024 |access-date=2025-02-01 |website=California Institute of Technology |language=en}}</ref> Anson attended a sophomore analytical chemistry course of Ernest Swift and also carried out electroanalytical chemical research in his laboratory. He spent his summers working at Harshaw Chemical Company, located near [[East Los Angeles, California|East Los Angeles]].<ref name=":1" /> 

Anson played for Caltech's basketball team for three years,<ref name="Scholar"/> and was the senior captain of the 1954 team, which secured the [[Southern California Intercollegiate Athletic Conference]] (SCIAC) championship.<ref name=":1" />

Anson received his bachelors at Caltech in 1954, PhD at [[Harvard University]] in 1957,<ref name="Wizards"/><ref>{{cite thesis |title=Studies in electrochemistry |first=Fred Colvig |last=Anson |year=1957 |institution=Harvard University |oclc=76978038 |id=<!--add ProQuest link here-->}}</ref> and worked in J. J. Lingane's research group with [[Allen J. Bard|Allen Bard]].<ref name=":2" /> Anson later worked at his Alma mater Caltech for the next 43 years.<ref name=":2" />

== Career ==
Anson completed a doctoral degree in chemistry from [[Harvard University]] in 1957, after which he returned to Caltech the same year as an instructor in the chemistry department.<ref name=":1" /><ref name="Wizards"/>

=== Research ===
Anson's area of research span [[chemical kinetics]], [[Electrochemical reaction mechanism|mechanisms]] and [[Electrocatalyst|catalysis of electrode reactions]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

Anson's initial studies focused on examining the electrochemical interactions of reactants bound to electrode surfaces. In the mid 1960s, he developed a method of using chronocoulometry to study electrode-attached reactants, presenting data in a format that would later become known as an Anson plot. In the mid-1960s, he created a technique utilizing [[Chronoamperometry#Chronocoulometry|chronocoulometry]] to analyze reactants attached to electrodes, presenting the results in a format that would later be referred to as an [[Anson equation|Anson plot]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=International Society of Electrochemistry |url=https://www.ise-online.org/obituary.php |access-date=2025-02-01 |website=www.ise-online.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250123080733/https://www.ise-online.org/obituary.php|archive-date=2025-01-23|url-status=deviated}}</ref> From 1970s to 90s, he investigated numerous surface-attached systems and was among the firsts in using thin polymer films to confine reactants at electrode surfaces. He also contributed to the understanding of [[Oxygen reduction reaction|electrocatalytic oxygen reduction]].<ref name=":2" />

=== Legacy ===
The National Academy of Sciences states that "Among his numerous impactful studies, he elucidated the electrochemistry of heteropolymetallates and catalysts for the electroreduction of dioxygen to water", a reaction occurring at the cathode of a fuel cell.<ref name=":1" />

Throughout his career, Anson received numerous prestigious awards, including:<ref name=":1" />

* The [[David Crockett Graham|David C. Grahame]] Award of the Electrochemical Society (the inaugural recipient)
* The C.N. Reilley Award in Electroanalytical Chemistry (1986)
* The [[American Chemical Society]] Award in Analytical Chemistry (1989)
* The [[Humboldt Research Award]] (1984), which enabled him to conduct research in Berlin

Anson was awarded a [[Guggenheim Fellow|Guggenheim fellowship]], and was a member of [[National Academy of Sciences]] and American Academy of Arts and Sciences.<ref name=":0" /> He was inducted into the National Academy of Sciences alongside neuroscientist [[Eugene Roberts (neuroscientist)|Eugene Roberts]] in 1988.<ref name="Wizards"/>

=== Other work ===
Anson, along with others, founded the Western Electrochemical and Technical Society, which held casual meetings to discuss electrochemistry on the beach in [[San Clemente, California|San Clemente]]. This group eventually turned into the Gordon Research Conference on Electrochemistry.<ref name=":2" /> 

Anson chaired the search committee for Caltech's next president for a year and a half. After an year and half, the committee selected [[Marvin Leonard Goldberger|Marvin L. Goldberger]] as the president.<ref name=":1" />

Anson was chairman of the faculty for two years, then became division chair for CCE in 1984.<ref name=":1" />

== Personal life ==
After Anson joined Caltech as an instructor in 1957, he felt that it was necessary to get an interlibrary loan, for which he was directed to meet Roxana, who worked in what was then the General Library. They married later in 1959.<ref name=":1" />
